posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: For extra stability and to reduce resonance of optical components for long exposures, one can use beeswax or modeling clay. Press the modeling clay into any joined pieces. As in around the base of the optic where the base meets the table. Or between the base and the pole or pole and optic holder etc... This should not be used alone to secure.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
You can also use the material that's sold for attaching posters to walls as your dampening helper. It's often sold under the name Blu-Tak (don't get the yellow stuff, it's greasy and too sticky).

I prefer this over clay as it doesn't leave any residue behind.

You can also attach blobs of it to the tops of mounts to prevent them from ringing.

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md: I like to use a hot melt glue gun to secure mirrors and optics. It can be removed and cleaned up easily.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: I like plasticine best: http://www.hobbycraft.com/product_searc ... Plasticine

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: Although all these techniques probably work well, I increase stability of components by attaching a second post (making a tripod) with a dab of 5-minute epoxy. It's cleaner than hot melt (no strings, wires or drooling of the gun), and wax (no residue on components or hands), and it picks off easily. The important thing is to do *something*, because most components pick up vibrations too easily on their own!

posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md:
i too am a big fan of plasticine and hotglue , i use the plasticine to secure objects and support glass film when making reflection holograms, by embedding a BB (or ball bearing) into the top of a small mound of plasticine and then do this three times to make a three point kinetic mount and simply drop my film plate on top and wait five min. and shoot!

i use hot glue to fasten down all my components, then i secure 3/8" dia

steel rods were i feel is needed

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: The best place I found for dampening is at the points where the plate meets the plate holder. I can instantly tell from the "tink" or "thunk" that the additional beeswax or whatever is working and adding dampening.
